source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Twelve theories of the syllogism were reviewed and seven were tested against pooled data from six studies. None gave an adequate account of human conclusions.
numbers: 12 theories reviewed, 7 scored (Euler circles, Venn, verbal substitution, monotonicity, source-founding dropped). Six data sets: Johnson-Laird and Steedman 1978 (2 tests, N=20 each), Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984 (N=20), Bara et al. 1995 (14-15 year olds N=20, adults N=20), Roberts et al. 2001 (N=56). 64 premise pairs, 27 valid, 37 with no valid conclusion.
quote: None of the 12 theories provides an adequate account
limits: Samples are small and from a few labs (US, Italy). Authors had the proponents check each theory's predictions.
agent_relevance: No single heuristic or rule explains syllogism errors, so a scaffold should not rely on one simple cue list. Use a real checker for validity.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: The pooled data are reliable: difficulty ranks agree across studies. So the errors are systematic, not noise.
numbers: Kendall W = .86 for the 27 valid syllogisms and W = .64 for the 37 no-valid-conclusion syllogisms. By-materials Wilcoxon: correct responses above chance for valid (z=3.94) and invalid (z=5.30), both p<.001. A response counted as reliable if it occurred in at least 16% of trials (chance 1/9).
limits: Agreement is on rank order, not on level. Level of accuracy differed by sample.
agent_relevance: Human error patterns are stable enough to use as a test set for model bias, not just accuracy.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Scoring each theory on hits (predicts what people say) and correct rejections (does not predict what people do not say) shows a trade-off. Mental models predict many responses but over-predict. Illicit conversion predicts few but rejects well.
numbers: Mental models: 95% hits, 74% correct rejections. Illicit conversion: 44% hits, 93% correct rejections. Verbal models (Polk and Newell): 63% hits, 90% correct rejections, best overall at 84% correct predictions (I2=52%, Q=10.69, p=.06, so partly heterogeneous). Model-based theories 76% vs heuristic-based 66% on aggregate correct predictions.
limits: Only one formal-rule theory (PSYCOP) was tested, so the rules-vs-models comparison is thin. Mental models showed small-sample publication bias in hits (z=2.03, p<.05). The aggregate of heuristics is below the best single theory.
agent_relevance: A conclusion generator that also checks for counterexamples (models plus a rejection step) fits people better than a pure heuristic. For an agent: generate, then search for a counterexample.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Problem difficulty varies from trivial to almost impossible, and hard problems are hard because people are unsure what to conclude, not because they agree on a wrong answer.
numbers: Easiest valid syllogism (All B are A; Some C are B): 90% correct. Hardest valid (All B are A; None of the C is B): 1% correct, most say None of the C is A. Easiest no-valid-conclusion item (None A are B; None C are B): 76% say nothing follows. Hardest (Some B are A; All C are B): 12% say nothing follows, most say Some C are A. Response entropy about 1 bit for easy items, over 2 bits for hard items.
limits: Percentages are pooled across six data sets with different instructions (absolute certainty vs follows necessarily).
agent_relevance: Choose test items by difficulty band. Entropy of a model's own sampled answers could flag the hard items where it should lean on a checker.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Individual differences are large, and the samples differ a lot. Figural bias (the order of terms in the premises) strongly shapes which valid conclusions people draw.
numbers: Columbia students drew 55% valid conclusions; students at a non-selective Italian university 37% (N=20 each). Individual range from 85% to 15% correct. When a valid conclusion fits the figural bias about 80% of people draw it; when it violates the bias about 20% do.
limits: Cited from earlier studies in the review, not recomputed. The review says the best account of the figural effect is semantic (Oberauer and colleagues).
agent_relevance: Order of terms in a prompt can change the model's answer. Test both A-B/B-C and B-A/C-B orderings and canonicalise before reasoning.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Atmosphere and illicit conversion are weak as full theories. Atmosphere covers about half of what people say but rejects most of what they do not say.
numbers: Atmosphere: 51% hits and 85% correct rejections. Conversion: 44% hits and 93% correct rejections (from the theory table).
limits: The pairing of rows in the extracted table is read from a layout-garbled PDF, so treat atmosphere's exact figures as likely but not certain.
agent_relevance: Atmosphere and conversion are cheap predictors of what a naive model will say. Useful as bias detectors, not as models of correct reasoning.

source: Khemlani (2020) Reasoning about syllogisms (chapter, modeltheory.org)
finding: Khemlani's later review says people use different strategies, build them during a session, and even the same person varies. Mental-model reasoning is described as a search for counterexamples in a model.
numbers: Repeats the meta-analysis data: some reasoners get 85% right and others 15%. A matching-type strategy predicted the stated conclusion 61% of the time on one pair (Iab Ibc), with about a third of responses otherwise.
limits: A chapter, not a new experiment. I read only parts of it.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one human reasoning procedure. Treat strategy as something the scaffold chooses, not something to copy.

source: Byrne (1989) suppression task data as tabulated in the cognitive argumentation paper (arXiv 2002.10149), with Dieussaert et al. (2000) replication
finding: Byrne (1989) suppression pattern, as tabulated in this paper: adding an additional requirement lowers modus ponens and modus tollens. Adding an alternative lowers denial of the antecedent and affirmation of the consequent.
numbers: Byrne 1989, percent drawing the conclusion. Plain group: MP 96, DA 46, AC 71, MT 92. Alternative group: MP 96, DA 4, AC 13, MT 96. Additional-requirement group: MP 38, DA 63, AC 54, MT 33.
limits: I could not open Byrne's original; the numbers are Table 1 of a secondary paper. Byrne's sample sizes are not given there. Column assignment follows the paper's layout and the known pattern.
agent_relevance: Valid inferences collapse when a plausible exception is mentioned. Logic-form checking alone will not match human-style answers; a defeasible reading changes the answer.

source: Byrne (1989) suppression task data as tabulated in the cognitive argumentation paper (arXiv 2002.10149), with Dieussaert et al. (2000) replication
finding: Dieussaert et al. (2000) replicated the suppression of modus ponens but with a smaller effect.
numbers: Plain / alternative / additional MP: Byrne 96 / 96 / 38; Dieussaert 88 / 93 / 60. DA in plain / alternative / additional: Byrne 46 / 4 / 63; Dieussaert 49 / 22 / 49. MT in additional group: Byrne 33, Dieussaert 44.
limits: Dieussaert's N is not shown in the extracted text. MP suppression falls from 58 points in Byrne to 28 points in the replication. Byrne restricted the permitted answers to a fixed set, which may have distorted results.
agent_relevance: Effect direction replicates, size is about half. Plan tests with a range of suppression sizes.

source: Byrne (1989) suppression task data as tabulated in the cognitive argumentation paper (arXiv 2002.10149), with Dieussaert et al. (2000) replication
finding: Competing explanation of suppression: not a failure of logic but a change in what the premises mean. In the additional-requirement group more people considered an outside explanation, so fewer concluded with certainty.
numbers: Share concluding with certainty in the additional-requirement group was significantly lower: 33% (Byrne) and 44% (Dieussaert), against 92% and 69% in the plain group for the same inference.
limits: A modelling paper: it fits the table but does not test new data. The Dieussaert rows in the extracted table are partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Suppression is context-sensitive reasoning. A scaffold should expose the exception check as an explicit step (is there a disabler?), not hide it.

source: De Neys, Schaeken, D'Ydewalle (2003) Inference suppression and semantic memory retrieval: every counterexample counts
finding: Suppression is graded: each extra counterexample lowers acceptance further. MP and MT fall with the number of disablers; AC and DA fall with the number of alternatives.
numbers: Exp 1: 178 first-year students, 4 discarded (88 in the alternatives group, 86 in the disablers group), 0 to 4 counterexamples shown. Negative linear trend for AC/DA with alternatives, F(1,87)=20.84, p<.0001; for MP F(1,85)=20.46 and MT F(1,85)=16.02 with disablers, both p<.001. Rating scale -5 to +5. Exp 2: 19 participants, counterexamples counted in a pretest, reasoning task one month later; same graded pattern.
limits: Ratings, not forced yes/no, and participants were not told to treat premises as certain. Results for DA and MT were less clear. Exp 2 N is small and people rarely generated many counterexamples.
agent_relevance: Acceptance can be modelled as a count of retrieved counterexamples. A counterexample search with a count could set a confidence instead of a yes/no.

source: De Neys, Schaeken, D'Ydewalle (2003) Inference suppression and semantic memory retrieval: every counterexample counts
finding: A side effect: presenting disablers raised acceptance of affirmation of the consequent, while presenting alternatives had no meaningful effect on modus ponens.
numbers: Disabler presentation raised AC acceptance, Rao R(4,82)=4.67, p<.002; for every number of disablers AC was higher than with none. Alternatives had no significant impact on MP.
limits: The materials analysis for AC had only five conditionals and did not reach significance, though the trend matched. The biconditional explanation was not tested here.
agent_relevance: Mentioning an exception can push a model toward the converse. Prompts that list exceptions may create AC errors.

source: Singmann, Klauer, Over (2014) New normative standards of conditional reasoning and the dual-source model
finding: The probability of 'if p then q' tracks the conditional probability P(q|p), not the conjunction or the material conditional, for believable everyday conditionals.
numbers: N=30 (mean age 22.4), each gave 4 responses per conditional. Raw correlation of P(if p then q) with P(q|p) r=.84; with P(p and q) r=.61. In a mixed model only P(q|p) mattered: b=.78, F(1,88.14)=86.81, p<.001; conjunction b=.00, p>.99; material conditional b=-.01, p=.91; P(q|not p) b=.00, p=.98. A three-way interaction was found, F(1,72.74)=4.09, p=.047.
limits: Highly believable, causal everyday conditionals only. Small N. Evans et al. (2007) finds a sizable conjunctive minority.
agent_relevance: When asking a model for confidence in an if-then claim, ask for P(q|p). The material reading (not p or q) is the wrong default.

source: Singmann, Klauer, Over (2014) New normative standards of conditional reasoning and the dual-source model
finding: Normative probability-logic standards fit modus ponens but not modus tollens. A dual-source model (background knowledge plus form-based belief) fits as well as a model fed only the probabilised task.
numbers: Responses were confidence-preserving (p-valid) for MP but not MT. Responses inside the mental-probability-logic coherence intervals exceeded chance mainly for MP and less so for DA. The form-based component was estimated from a second, abstract-content deductive task with strong deduction instructions.
limits: N=30 and a single-site design. Exact coherence rates were not extracted.
agent_relevance: People use two sources: content knowledge and form. An agent can do the same on purpose: score the form check and the knowledge check separately and combine in code.

source: Evans, Handley, Neilens, Over (2007) Thinking about conditionals: a study of individual differences
finding: People split into two kinds: those who judge a conditional by conditional probability and those who judge by conjunctive probability. The conditional-probability group has higher general ability.
numbers: N=120 (115 classified). Conjunctive group n=46, conditional group n=69. AH4 score 91.65 (SD 14.29) vs 98.07 (SD 12.67), t=2.45, p=.013. Conjunctive responders also accepted more AC inferences.
limits: Abstract conditionals, a 10-minute AH4 test that gives no population-normed IQ, student sample.
agent_relevance: Two readings of 'if' coexist even in one sample. An agent interpreting a user's 'if' should keep both readings or ask.

source: Evans, Handley, Neilens, Over (2007) Thinking about conditionals: a study of individual differences
finding: Conditional inference rates on abstract rules show the standard asymmetries, and negation changes the rates (negation effects).
numbers: N=120, percent endorsing. 'If p then q': MP 100, DA 55, AC 74, MT 61. 'If p then not-q': MP 99, DA 37, AC 68, MT 64. 'If not-p then q': MP 96, DA 55, AC 81, MT 35. 'If not-p then not-q': MP 95, DA 40, AC 74, MT 39.
limits: Abstract materials. MT is lower for rules with a negated antecedent, which is a double-negation difficulty.
agent_relevance: MT with a negated antecedent in the rule is the weak spot (35% to 39%). Normalise the negations in code before reasoning.

source: Evans, Handley, Neilens, Over (2007) Thinking about conditionals: a study of individual differences
finding: Higher-ability participants endorse fewer fallacies (DA, AC) but not more MT, which complicates the claim that ability makes people more logical.
numbers: For affirmative conditionals, DA rates (t=2.63, p<.01) and AC rates (t=2.81, p<.01) were significantly lower in the high-ability group. MP and MT differences were small and nonsignificant; MT trended lower in high-ability people, as in Newstead et al. (2004). AH4 correlated r=.25 (p<.01) with the false-antecedent index.
limits: Ability split within one sample. The MT trend is not significant here.
agent_relevance: A stronger reasoner may block invalid inferences yet still miss MT. Check MT separately.

source: Skovgaard-Olsen, Singmann, Klauer (2016) The relevance effect and conditionals
finding: The Equation P(if A, then C) = P(C|A) is moderated by relevance: when the antecedent is irrelevant or negatively relevant to the consequent, the slope on P(C|A) drops.
numbers: Online sample, 577 completed, 348 kept. Slope of P(if A then C) on P(C|A): positive relevance b=0.78 (CI .71 to .85), negative relevance b=0.61 (CI .52 to .71), irrelevance b=0.43 (CI .35 to .52). PO vs NE t(41.53)=3.26; PO vs IR t(53.13)=6.22, p<.0001. Some individuals had slopes near zero in the irrelevance condition.
limits: Large exclusion (577 to 348). Vignette scenarios, 12 within-subject conditions. The Default and Penalty Hypothesis is the authors' own explanation.
agent_relevance: A conditional that is probable but irrelevant ('if blood is red, then 2+2=4') is judged badly. Add a relevance check on if-claims before using P(q|p).

source: Skovgaard-Olsen, Singmann, Klauer (2016) The relevance effect and conditionals
finding: Concessive conditionals ('even if A, then still C') follow the Equation better than ordinary indicatives across relevance conditions.
numbers: Same experiment: the Equation fit concessive conditionals better than indicative ones across the positive, negative and irrelevance conditions.
limits: Detailed concessive slope numbers were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Phrase 'even if' differently from 'if' in prompts, since they invoke different reasoning.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: LLMs avoid 'nothing follows'. In-context learning does not fix this even with same-schema examples; supervised fine-tuning does.
numbers: Zero-shot chain-of-thought, Pythia and LLaMA. Human accuracy 44.63% valid and 40.97% invalid. Best invalid accuracy: LLaMA-3 70B instruct 32.50%. SFT puts both Pythia and LLaMA at or near ceiling on valid and invalid items. Instruction tuning raised invalid accuracy but lowered valid.
limits: Fine-tuned on the same 64 schemas with pseudo-words, so ceiling may be pattern matching, as the authors say.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only scaffold cannot be expected to teach 'nothing follows'; use a validity checker or counterexample search for the NVC decision.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: Atmosphere theory predicts what zero-shot LLaMA-3 8B says, which would explain why it rarely says nothing follows.
numbers: Atmosphere predicts 92.31% of LLaMA ZS-CoT correct valid conclusions and 82.97% of its mistakes on invalid and 62.79% on valid schemas. For comparison, atmosphere predicts 62.50% of the correct conclusions to valid schemas and 0% on invalid schemas in general.
limits: One 8B model for the main analysis. Atmosphere is a weak human theory per Khemlani and Johnson-Laird.
agent_relevance: A cheap bias check: does the model's conclusion mood simply match the premise moods?

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: In-context examples raise contradictory answers; fine-tuning reduces them for the larger model but not for the smaller one.
numbers: Contradictory answers (all/some-not, none/some, or NVC plus another). LLaMA-3 8B: ZS-CoT 1.09%, ICL-out 1.72%, ICL-in 3.12%, SFT 0.31%. Pythia-1.4B: ZS-CoT 18.91%, ICL-out 28.12%, ICL-in 28.28%, SFT 73.91% (70.47% from 'nothing follows' plus another conclusion).
limits: Consistency measured only on believable syllogisms. Only two model families.
agent_relevance: Check set consistency in code: a model that says 'nothing follows' and also gives a conclusion is wrong on one of them.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: Longer premise chains hurt. Content effects remained in zero-shot and in-context settings; only fine-tuning removed them.
numbers: 280 items each for 3-premise and 4-premise sets (an A-premise replaced by a chain). Zero-shot accuracy falls as the chain grows; ICL-out is more robust than ICL-in; SFT is best but drops more than ICL. 640 believable and 270 unbelievable items (27 valid schemas x 10 term triples).
limits: Per-condition chain accuracies were in a table I read only in part.
agent_relevance: Break long premise chains into pairwise steps and verify each step; abstract terms help against content effects.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: Larger PaLM 2 models beat humans on syllogism accuracy but still show human-like errors: an ordering effect and the same fallacy items.
numbers: Human accuracy averaged about 50%; the best LM about 75%; the two largest models exceed humans. Scale did not always help (the largest model was somewhat below the second largest; on some items such as EA1 accuracy fell with size). All four PaLM 2 sizes show the premise-ordering effect in the human direction, with a moderately larger bias than humans. The top three human fallacies are also outliers for the models.
limits: PaLM 2 with a Llama 2 replication. Zero-shot chain-of-thought used 75 decoded tokens at temperature 0.5; a step-by-step prompt gave moderately higher accuracy.
agent_relevance: Even strong models inherit figural bias; reorder premises as a diagnostic.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: LMs rarely answer 'nothing follows', far more rarely than humans, even when it is the only correct answer.
numbers: On the 37 syllogisms whose only valid answer is 'nothing follows', model accuracy is close to 0% (zero-shot chain-of-thought). On one fallacy item the correct conclusion was produced 3% of the time. An alternative elicitation method is described in Appendix B.3.
limits: Prompt format matters; the appendix paradigm can elicit the answer. Humans are also reluctant to say it (Ragni et al., 2019).
agent_relevance: Score and handle NVC explicitly; ask 'what would a counterexample look like?' as a separate query.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: Fitting the mReasoner mental-model simulator to the LMs: larger models look more deliberative (System 2) even in their errors.
numbers: 1296 mReasoner models over a parameter grid, 923 finished; first principal component captures 77% of variance and correlates with accuracy. In a control where the correct answer's probability is set to 0, PC 1 has zero correlation with accuracy but correlation 0.6 with the System-2 parameter; other parameters under 0.15.
limits: Fits come from a simulator with a hand-set parameter space. Reading it as 'deliberation' is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Counterexample search (System 2) is what scale seems to buy; a scaffold can supply it to a small model through code.

source: Ando et al. (2023) Evaluating large language models with NeuBAROCO: syllogistic reasoning ability and human-like biases
finding: On the NeuBAROCO English and Japanese syllogism set, models did worse when the conclusion conflicted with belief, on conversion items and on atmosphere items.
numbers: GPT-3.5 overall 51.73%; entailment 79.51%, contradiction 38.03%, neutral 38.46%. Symbol / belief-consistent / belief-inconsistent: 61.05%, 56.89%, 31.37%. Atmosphere items: GPT-3.5 39.42%, fine-tuned NLI models 0% and 0.96%. RoBERTa overall 34.67%, with 0.55% on neutral.
limits: Old models (GPT-3.5, RoBERTa, BART), no chain-of-thought. Some numbers read from a text-form table may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Includes labelled conversion and atmosphere subsets that we could reuse as tests for S4.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: empowering large language models with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: Offloading deduction to a symbolic solver beats standard and chain-of-thought prompting on most logic benchmarks, with one exception.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy, Standard / CoT / Logic-LM: PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20; ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. With GPT-3.5 the average gain over standard prompting is 39.2% and over CoT 18.4%.
limits: Not syllogism-specific. On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beat Logic-LM (83.20), partly because translation into a formal language can fail. Solver pipelines depend on the program being executable.
agent_relevance: A solver (Prover9, Z3) for the final validity check fits guardrail G3. Keep a fallback when translation fails.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models show the human belief-bias pattern on syllogism validity judgements and are strongly affected by content.
numbers: Both humans and LMs show moderate accuracy and substantial content effects on validity judgements. Cited human figure: people mistakenly call an invalid syllogism valid about 90% of the time when the conclusion is believable (from Evans et al. 1983).
limits: Overlaps the earlier belief_bias document; the setting is validity judgement, not conclusion generation. I read only the syllogism section.
agent_relevance: See the belief-bias file; kept here to tie the NeuBAROCO and Bertolazzi results together.
